introduction: One moment your cat is leaning into your hand. The next, teeth appear. Was that affection, an invitation to play, or a request to stop? A single gesture rarely tells the whole story.

Cats communicate through small changes in posture, touch and sound. Looking at the whole interaction can help you notice the quieter signs of trust—and understand when your pet would rather have some space.
gallery.completeCopy: Notice the context, respect their boundaries and let affection happen on their terms.

items.title: That Bite Is Not Automatically a Love Bite
paragraphs: A bite during stroking can mean that contact has become uncomfortable. Some cats enjoy a little attention but reach their limit quickly. Play, fear or pain can also be involved, so the bite alone cannot tell you what your cat feels.

Look for what happened just before it: a flicking tail, tense body, ears turning back or an attempt to move away. Stop touching, allow space and avoid punishment. A relaxed moment can change, and continuing to stroke is not a useful way to test the message.

items.title: The Slow Blink: A Quiet Sign of Comfort
paragraphs: Soft eyes and a slow closing of the eyelids, paired with relaxed posture, can be part of calm social communication. It is a quieter signal than running over for a cuddle, but still worth noticing.
Try softening your gaze and slowly blinking back rather than staring. Your cat does not need to copy you for the moment to count as a pleasant interaction. Let them look away or leave.

items.title: Head Bumps and Cheek Rubs Make You Familiar
paragraphs: When a cat presses their forehead or cheek against you, touch and scent work together. Cats have scent glands around the head, and friendly rubbing helps create a familiar shared scent.

A gentle head bump can be a social greeting, not just a demand for food. Notice whether your cat stays loose and chooses to repeat the contact. Let them guide the interaction instead of holding them in place.

items.title: Kneading Can Be a Comfortable Throwback
paragraphs: The rhythmic pushing of paws against a blanket or lap starts in kittenhood, when kittens knead during feeding. In adult cats, it can accompany a settled, contented state.

If claws make the moment uncomfortable, put a soft blanket between you and the paws or give your cat another comfortable surface. There is no need to punish a behaviour associated with feeling secure.

items.title: Choosing to Sleep Near You Can Show Trust
paragraphs: Sleeping leaves a cat less ready to react. Choosing your lap, the end of the bed or a nearby resting spot can suggest that your presence feels safe enough to relax around.
Not every trusting cat wants to sleep on a person. Warmth, comfort and individual preference also influence the choice. A cat resting nearby can enjoy your company without wanting constant touch.

items.title: A Tail-Up Greeting Is Worth Noticing
paragraphs: A cat approaching with an upright tail and a gently curved tip may be offering a friendly greeting. Read it alongside an easy posture and relaxed face, rather than treating tail position as a complete translation.
Let the cat approach. A greeting does not commit them to being picked up, and a tail that starts lashing during contact can mean the mood has changed.

items.title: Showing a Belly Is Not a Belly-Rub Invitation
paragraphs: Rolling onto the back in a relaxed interaction can indicate comfort and trust. But exposing a vulnerable area is not the same as inviting you to touch it.

Many cats would rather keep hands away from their stomach. Enjoy the relaxed greeting without reaching in. Trust is easier to maintain when your cat can show comfort without having their boundaries tested.

items.title: Purring Needs Context Too
paragraphs: A purr beside you, with a loose body and soft eyes, may fit a contented moment. But cats can also purr when stressed or in pain, so the sound is not proof that everything is fine.
Look at the rest of the picture. A tense, withdrawn cat needs a different response from one calmly choosing contact. New or worrying changes deserve attention even if the cat is still purring.

items.title: The Best Affection Leaves Room for ‘Enough’
paragraphs: Keep contact brief and give your cat a chance to choose whether to continue. Avoid uninvited handling, restraint or trying to force a cuddle when they want to move away.

Stop at signs of irritation rather than waiting for a bite. Calm, predictable interactions make it easier to respect an individual cat's limits. Hands and feet should not become toys during rough play.

items.title: Know When to Ask for Help
paragraphs: Sudden biting, new sensitivity to touch or a clear change in normal behaviour can have a medical cause. Speak to a veterinarian instead of assuming your cat has become unfriendly. This article offers general information, not an assessment of your pet.

If a bite breaks your skin, wash it with soap and warm water and seek medical advice promptly, especially for a bite to the hand or any signs of infection. A large or deep wound, or bleeding that will not stop, needs urgent medical care.
